title: Krishna runs at Bhishma
hookLine: Krishna promised not to fight. Then he jumps down from the chariot and runs at Bhishma, and Bhishma welcomes him.
carry: bhakta vatsala: god bends for his devotees

cards: A charioteer's work is the reins. Krishna came to this war with one promise: he would not take up a weapon. He drives the chariot, he talks, and in the Gita he taught.
But he doesn't fight. Then, early in the battle, Bhishma is cutting through the Pandava ranks, and Arjuna is holding back. And Krishna leaps down from the chariot and runs at Bhishma on foot.
Today: the day the driver breaks his word, and the man he runs at welcomes him.

teach.b: Duryodhana has accused Bhishma of going easy on the Pandavas, and the old man is stung. So he fights like fire. And Arjuna, facing the grandfather he grew up with, fights gently; he can't make himself strike hard.
Krishna sees the Pandava army breaking. He drops the reins, jumps down, and rushes at Bhishma with his discus raised. Bhishma doesn't flinch.
He stands his ground, bow in hand, and calls out a welcome. Come, strike me down. To be killed by you would be an honor.
Then Arjuna jumps down after Krishna, grabs him, and holds on, dragged along the ground until Krishna stops. Arjuna swears he'll fight in earnest, and Krishna climbs back into the chariot.
Days later, it happens again, this time with nothing in Krishna's hand but his horse whip.
Bhishma welcomes him again. Arjuna pulls him back again. Now hear why devotees love this scene.

teach.h: BHAKTA VATSALA: GOD BENDS FOR HIS DEVOTEES
teach.b: Krishna is called bhakta vatsala: tender toward his devotees. Many teachers read the charge this way: God would rather bend his own word than watch the people who love him fall. And look at Bhishma.

In the Bhagavata Purana, as he lies dying, his last praise of Krishna remembers this very moment: Krishna, he says, set aside his own promise to make Bhishma's promise come true. The enemy commander is a devotee too.
In Hindu bhakti, devotion, love runs both ways, and it can find you even on a battlefield.

how: The scene of Krishna leaping from the chariot toward Bhishma is told in the Bhishma book of the Mahabharata, remembered in Bhishma's dying praise in the Bhagavata Purana, and loved by devotees as a picture of Krishna as bhakta vatsala.

games.q: you're Arjuna. your driver, who promised not to fight, has jumped down and is running at your grandfather. what do you do?
o: let him go: Bhishma has to be stopped.
jump down, grab him, and promise to fight in earnest.
games.why: Arjuna jumps down and holds on until Krishna stops, then swears to fight properly. Krishna climbs back into the chariot.

practice: This week began with a man sitting down in his chariot and ends with God jumping out of one. Bhishma met that moment with welcome.

Breathing in, bring to mind one way you were loved this week, by God, if you pray, or by someone who went out of their way for you. Breathing out, offer a quiet thank you. If you pray, let it become your prayer.
If you don't, let the thanks be enough.

wordCard.voice: Bhishma's fall. Still not yet. Today it's a man so devoted that he welcomes the one who comes to bring his death.

orig.note: bhakta vatsala, tender toward devotees: a name for Krishna, who bends his own vow for those who love him.

carryVoice: Your line: bhakta vatsala: God bends for his devotees. Twice the driver ran, and the man he ran at welcomed him. See you tomorrow.
